sentences.text: Soroavisaurus belongs to the bird family Avisauridae.
All known fossils of this animal consist exclusively of hind limb bones.
The tarsometatarsus is a slender bone formed by the fusion of tarsal and metatarsal bones only in the upper portion.
Metatarsal IV is flattened and slender, creating a distinct gap between it and metatarsal III in the upper part of the tarsometatarsus.
This separation between the third and fourth metatarsals is a unique defining feature of Soroavisaurus not found in other enantiornithines.
The trochlea of metatarsal IV has a triangular outline with a bony projection that nearly seals the gap between metatarsals III and IV.
The first toe consists of two phalanges forming a sharp, curved talon.
The holotype specimen PVL-4690 is a left tarsometatarsus measuring 46.9 mm in length.
Specimen PVL-4048 includes a 51.5 mm left tarsometatarsus associated with the hallux and four toe bones.
Soroavisaurus is estimated to have been about 40 cm long, though size variation suggests some individuals were larger.
The species Soroavisaurus australis was named in 1993.
The genus Soroavisaurus was named by Luis M. Chiappe in 1993.
All known specimens of Soroavisaurus are fossilized leg bones found at El Brete in the Salta province of Argentina.
The fossil deposits of the Lecho Formation at El Brete were discovered in 1975 by a team from the Fundación Miguel Lillo.
In 1981, Cyril Walker identified the bird fossils from El Brete as belonging to the group Enantiornithes.
The only known species, Soroavisaurus australis, is known from fossils collected from the Lecho Formation in Estancia El Brete, southern Salta Province, Argentina.

The fossil record includes specimen PVL-4690, a left tarsometatarsus 46.9 mm long, and PVL-4048, a left tarsometatarsus 51.5 mm long associated with an incomplete hallux and four intermediate phalanges.
Specimen PVL-4048 was previously described as "Avisaurus sp." before being assigned to Soroavisaurus.
Soroavisaurus is hypothesized to have been a perching carnivore occupying an ecological niche similar to modern birds of prey.
Soroavisaurus is classified as an extinct member of the avian clade Enantiornithes.
Soroavisaurus is placed in the family Avisauridae as a close relative of the North American genus Avisaurus.
A 2024 study revised the family Avisauridae to include only six members, excluding genera previously thought to belong to it.
Recent research suggests Intiornis is a more basal relative of the group leading to Avisauridae rather than the closest relative of Soroavisaurus.
Soroavisaurus is considered to occupy a basal position within the family Avisauridae.
Soroavisaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 71 to 69 million years ago.
Soroavisaurus lived in the Maastrichtian age on a warm, humid coastal plain featuring tropical forests, ponds, and lagoons.
All known specimens of Soroavisaurus come from the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous period.
The Lecho Formation deposits containing Soroavisaurus are estimated to be between 71 and 69 million years old.
The environment at El Brete where Soroavisaurus lived was a coastal plain dotted with ponds and lagoons.
The habitat near the Tropic of Capricorn featured a humid, warm climate supporting coastal tropical forests.
The time range for Soroavisaurus is estimated from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Soroavisaurus is the same species as Enantiornis or Martinavis, though confirmation is difficult due to the lack of overlapping fossil parts.
A 2007 study suggested that Soroavisaurus might be a junior synonym of Enantiornis.
Researchers note that it is difficult to determine if wing fossils belong to Soroavisaurus, and some suggest a Martinavis species might represent its wings instead of Enantiornis.
The exact position of Soroavisaurus within the family Avisauridae is debated, with some authors placing it as an early-diverging member rather than close to North American forms like Avisaurus.
